paper_metadata.title: Microstructure and mechanical properties of a novel Nb–V–Ce multi-microalloyed low-alloy cast steel

evidence.quote: A novel Nb–V–Ce multi-microalloyed low-alloy cast steel for offshore platform nodes was investigated to achieve the properties similar to X80 pipeline steel, including high yield strength and low-temperature impact energy.
Microstructure and mechanical properties of a novel Nb–V–Ce multi-microalloyed low-alloy cast steel
The addition of microalloying elements and the optimization of Si lead to a significant increase in strength, while also influencing the low-temperature impact toughness of low-alloy cast steel

The cast steels with different alloy and microalloy compositions were produced using a 10-kg medium frequency induction furnace in combination with the sand casting method. The chemical compositions of the cast steels are presented in Table 1. For clarity in further discussion, they are labeled as 0.6Si–0Nb–0V, 0.6Si–0.04Nb–0.05V and 0.3Si–0.04Nb–0.05V, respectively.

The microstructure of 0.6Si–0Nb–0V cast steel consists of tempered martensite and a minor amount of ferrite (Fig. 2g).
The microstructure of 0.6Si–0Nb–0V cast steel consists of tempered martensite and a minor amount of ferrite (Fig. 2g).
With the addition of 0.04 wt.% Nb, 0.05 wt.% V and 0.02 wt.% Ce, the width of martensite lath in 0.6Si–0.04Nb–0.05V steel decreases (Fig. 2h).

Upon reducing Si content to 0.28 wt.%, the microstructure of 0.3Si–0.04Nb–0.05V steel retains tempered martensite and block ferrite, with the tempered martensite displaying a shift toward equiaxed grains (Fig. 2i).

Upon reducing Si content to 0.28 wt.%, the microstructure of 0.3Si–0.04Nb–0.05V steel retains tempered martensite and block ferrite, with the tempered martensite displaying a shift toward equiaxed grains (Fig. 2i).

evidence.quote: The excellent mechanical properties of the multi-microalloyed low-alloy cast steel result from the reason that the multi-addition of microalloying elements refines the grains and facilitates the formation of nanoprecipitates like NbC.
In addition, with the addition of microalloying elements, the width of martensitic lath also decreases, which is consistent with the trend of grain size in Fig. 2.

In addition, compared to 0.6Si–0Nb–0V and 0.6Si–0.04Nb–0.05V steels, 0.3Si–0.04Nb–0.05V steel exhibits a more prominent tendency toward equiaxed martensite laths (Fig. 3e, f), consistent with OM image results (Fig. 2h, i).

This shift suggests that microalloying elements play a crucial role in promoting grain refinement, while the impact of Si on grain size is minimal (Fig. 2e, f).

These results suggest that the addition of microalloying elements promotes precipitation, while a decrease in Si content not only enhances the equiaxation tendency of the matrix but also induces some coarsening of precipitates.
Moreover, decreasing Si content can enhance the recovery of martensitic laths in cast steel during the tempering process, reducing stress from dislocation movement and improving plasticity.
When the content of microalloying elements remains constant, and Si content decreases from 0.63 to 0.28 wt.%, the size of nanoprecipitates in 0.3Si–0.04Nb–0.0V steel increases (Fig. 3i).
The interplay between Si solid-solution strengthening and stacking fault energy results in a decreased critical strain at the initiation of mechanical twinning
